title: Requirements: User, Content, Data, Quality, and Constraint
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Requirements: User, Content, Data, Quality, and Constraint. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Requirements describe what a product or service must enable and the conditions it must satisfy. They can be user requirements, functional behaviours, content needs, data needs, quality attributes, operational constraints, accessibility commitments, legal obligations, or business boundaries. Good requirements retain a trace to evidence and a reason to exist.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Separate requirement from implementation. “A person can confirm or reschedule from the reminder” expresses a necessary capability. “Send an SMS with two buttons” is one possible implementation. This distinction preserves room to explore alternatives and makes review more rigorous.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Quality requirements deserve equal status. Reliability, privacy, accessibility, response time, recovery, and clarity are not polish added after core behaviour. They determine whether the nominal capability is safe and usable in reality.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a balanced requirement set?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: User requirements describe outcomes and capabilities in context. Functional requirements describe system behaviour. Content requirements specify meaning, source, structure, ownership, and lifecycle. Data requirements cover fields, quality, lineage, permissions, retention, and states.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Quality attributes cover accessibility, performance, reliability, security, privacy, safety, and usability. Constraints identify policy, technology, budget, time, and operations.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Trace each to evidence and consequence. State measurable acceptance while avoiding false precision. “Respond within two seconds for 95% of eligible requests under defined load” is testable; “fast” is not. Include errors, absence, concurrency, translation, third parties, and recovery.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Resolve conflicts as product decisions. Stronger verification may affect access and time; richer data may affect privacy; consistency may conflict with expert flexibility. Record owner, rationale, residual risk, and validation method.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Maintain requirements with version and change impact. A requirement that cannot explain why it exists becomes difficult to challenge and easy to obey after the original need has disappeared.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Make quality measurable without pretending certainty
turns.text: What changes when we look at make quality measurable without pretending certainty?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Replace adjectives with conditions and evidence. “Fast” becomes a response distribution for a named operation, network profile, and percentile. “Accessible” points to the applicable standard and adds task-based testing with disabled participants. “Understandable” becomes accurate explanation and next-action selection in realistic scenarios.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Numbers should express a defensible threshold, not manufacture confidence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Prioritisation must consider consequence and dependency, not only request volume. A rare duplicate-booking race may deserve attention because clinical capacity and patient trust are at stake. Record what is deferred, who bears the risk, and what signal triggers reconsideration.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at convert needs into testable conditions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Each requirement links to source evidence, owner, priority, acceptance method, and consequence if wrong. Conflicts—speed versus clinical review, personalisation versus privacy—are resolved explicitly rather than hidden in a backlog item. A clinical constraint may be fixed; a duplicated evidence request may only be inherited habit.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at write requirements as traceable agreements?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Content requirements specify message purpose, required meaning, hierarchy, variables, states, channel, and governance. Data requirements specify definition, source, freshness, validity, missingness, permissions, and lineage. Service requirements describe staff authority, handoff, capacity, escalation, and evidence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Constraints are classified as law, safety, policy, contract, technology, capacity, or choice so they can be challenged appropriately.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Conflicts are resolved at the requirement level. Personalisation may conflict with minimisation; instant feedback may conflict with authoritative distributed state; a short form may conflict with necessary evidence. The decision record names the trade-off and guardrail. Requirements remain connected to scenarios, workflow, design, tests, and production measures.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: delivery address?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Collect a valid address” is incomplete. The product needs country formats, building access, delivery instructions, privacy, autocomplete limitations, manual entry, validation source, and recovery when a technically valid address is operationally unreachable.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Trace each requirement to a source: user evidence, policy, operational reality, technical constraint, or strategic decision. Untraced requirements tend to become permanent assumptions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Add appointment reminders” sounds like a requirement. It is a solution. The actual requirement may include a patient’s need to prepare, a clinic’s need to reduce no-shows, consent for reminders, a reliable contact method, accessible message content, a reschedule route, and a rule about when contact is appropriate.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Worked example For appointment reminders, user need is timely understandable notice and a viable change path. Content requires date, location, preparation, sender, and next action from authoritative sources. Data requires current contact preference and appointment state. Quality covers delivery, accessibility, privacy, and latency.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Policy defines when rescheduling is allowed; operations define capacity. A reminder screen alone satisfies only one slice of the requirement system. lesson 108 clarified the artifacts used to communicate intent. This lesson makes their content complete enough to guide design and delivery. lesson 110 offers the reusable decision tools that help apply those requirements.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Pick a feature statement. Rewrite it into one user, one quality, one data/content, and one constraint requirement—without naming a particular UI.
